problem.statement: Trisect an arbitrary given angle using only an unmarked straightedge and compass in a finite number of steps.

approach.summary: Search for a finite compass-and-straightedge construction that divides any given angle into three equal parts.

failure.point: Trisecting a general angle (e.g. 60°) requires solving an irreducible cubic, producing a number of degree 3 over the rationals, which is not constructible because constructible numbers have degree a power of 2.
failure.evidence: Proven impossible by Pierre Wantzel (1837) using field theory; a standard result in abstract algebra (constructible numbers lie in a tower of quadratic extensions).

environment.description: Classical Euclidean construction with an unmarked straightedge and compass.

transferability.notes: The impossibility is for a general angle with the classical tools only. Specific angles (90°, 45°) are trisectable, and relaxing the tools (marked ruler/neusis, origami) makes trisection possible.

confidence.notes: Settled theorem (Wantzel, 1837); the "reproduction" is the proof, not an experiment.
